doc.title: Buster Williams interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

chapter: Growing up with his father's music
title: Playing gigs with his father and Philadelphia cabarets
summary: He describes club dates, dances and parties with his father, jazz being accessible then, and the Seven Eleven ballroom cabarets with Jimmy Heath.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: What kind of work was it? What kind of gigs was he playing, that he would take you out on? Were they club dates? Just dances? Things like that?
And were you playing jazz at that time?

Um hum. Yeah. But you know jazz in those days I mean it was accessible to everybody and everybody loved it. I mean it wasn’t pigeon-holed. I mean we used to play [sings] “Straighten up and fly right — Straighten up and fly right — Straighten up and fly right

—Cool down, Papa don’t you blow your top.” You know? And on the breaks my father used to spin his bass and catch it back in time for the next downbeat. But the music was intellectual but it didn’t exclude anyone. And of course the big bands were popping and thriving and I mean you went to a dance and you had a live band. You used to play a lot of cabarets and people used to bring their own liquor and they’d have a table and they’d just order a set up. Remember cabarets?
Well not like that I guess.

Yeah, we used to have this big place in Philadelphia called the Seven Eleven. And it was a ballroom. And they’d have two bands, in fact one of my first gigs was with Jimmy Heath at one of these cabarets. Jimmy Heath was one band, and Sam Wied was the other band, all Philadelphia musicians. And your reservation — you’d have your own table and a big party of people come for your table. There was a big ballroom, and you bring your own liquor. And what they would serve you there at the ballroom would be ginger ale, ice, all of the things that you needed to go along with your liquor.
I see. And that was called the set up.
That was the set up. Potato chips and all that kind of stuff. And the cabarets happened every weekend. So I played a lot of those kind of things.
